title: I want my game to be deep, but 25 of my 58 players left within 15 minutes. How do you keep complexity without scaring people off?
author: Curious_Ad5417
selftext:
I'm making a dark fantasy keep builder and the depth is on purpose. 60 beasts to hunt, a keep that grows over 30 levels, gear in six rarities you can forge, harden and fuse, guilds with a shared castle that gets besieged, an arena with four leagues and a story told in chapters.

I've been playing games for over 30 years, but I'm not someone who plays many. When I pick one, I stay with it for years. So I'm building the game I always wanted, out of the things that kept me hooked all that time.

But my numbers are clear. 25 of my 58 players left within the first 15 minutes. The ones who stay seem to like exactly that depth, about 4 in 10 come back the next day.

I already made the start much simpler. One short intro page, a clear first goal, everything else hidden until you need it. Still, at some point the game opens up and it is a lot.

So the real question for me isn't how to make it simpler. It's how to make a complex game feel welcoming. Do you lock systems for days? Let people ignore most of it? Teach through the story?

How do you handle this in your games?

For anyone curious how it's made, I code with Claude, the art comes from ChatGPT image generation with a fixed style guide, and the town and characters are rendered in Blender. If you want to try it, it's free in the browser, no account needed: [https://grauwacht.com/start?von=reddit-aig2](https://grauwacht.com/start?von=reddit-aig2) [https://grauwacht.com/start?von=reddit-aig2](https://grauwacht.com/start?von=reddit-aig2)

comments.author: Outrageous-Issue9722
comments.body: Getting 58 people to even play your game is already an achievement these days to be honest.  Don't cater to the people who don't stick around by making things easier, lean hard into the ones that do stick around.. they stick around for a reason! And chances are the ones who left, it just wasn't their kind of game and nothing you do would get them to stay

replies.author: Curious_Ad5417
replies.body: Thats honestly a relief to read. The ones who stay are exactly the players Im building it for, so maybe the goal isn't keeping everyone, just making sure the right people find out fast that it's their kind of game. Do you think that's more about what you show in the first minutes, or about how the game presents itself before you even start?

replies.author: Outrageous-Issue9722
replies.body: A bit of both, if your game has deep systems you don't want to throw it in their face all at once, but you do want to ease them into it.  I didn't play your game so can only go off what you said, but in your sawmill example: maybe start them off with some simpler building before throwing building a sawmill at them? That way people can go "oh, this is how you build things" instead of "how do I even approach this"

replies.author: Curious_Ad5417
replies.body: Thats pretty much what I changed this week. The sawmill used to be the very first task, now you start with a short hunt that plays out on the map, and building comes after youve seen what the game is about. Glad to hear it from someone outside, it means I'm not just guessing.

replies.author: AceHighness
replies.body: I was gonna say everything he said :) 58 testers is amazing .. maybe you can add more in game telemetry so you can find out more details about what works and what doesn't, or at which point exactly some players exit.

replies.author: Melodic-Chemistry127
replies.body: This(and the previous comment). Add telemetry and maybe introduce complexity progressively instead of all at once if you can.

replies.author: Curious_Ad5417
replies.body: Both good points, and I do track it. The clearest number so far, of my 58 players, 33 never got past the very first task of the old tutorial, which was building a sawmill. That's why I changed the start this week. And yes, progressive is the plan, most systems stay hidden until your keep reaches the level where they make sense. The question is how fast to open them up.

replies.author: Melodic-Chemistry127
replies.body: Wanna DM me a copy? I can take a look. Maybe in return, you can play my game in the future for 10 minutes once it's ready.

replies.author: Curious_Ad5417
replies.body: Deal! No copy needed, it runs right in the browser, the link is at the bottom of the post. Just start fresh and tell me where it got confusing or boring. And yes, ping me when yours is ready, 10 minutes is the least I can do.

replies.author: Melodic-Chemistry127
replies.body:
Ok, I gave it a shot. For me personally, I don't know why I'm upgrading the keep or whatnot. I know I will probably get more resources, but what am I getting them for? 

The chest opening after each upgrade feels like a chore after a while. Better to give a bigger chest less often. Other chest rewards are scattered in other menus as well(the scroll).

Combat should be much faster - both the animations and the delays between hits.

Then at some point, relatively early in the game, I just hit a wall of waiting and idk why I'd want to come back and check the tab again. Maybe it could work for a mobile game where I check it once a day while I'm waiting for something?

Also, what's the point of all the resources? They feel just like numbers I don't care about. I had to choose a reward early between multiple resources, but how am I supposed to know or care what I want.

  
I don't intend to be mean, btw. Just my very unfiltered opinions. Hope at least some of them are going to be useful.

replies.author: Curious_Ad5417
replies.body: Thank you, this is exactly the kind of unfiltered feedback I need, and none of it reads as mean. A few of these I'm already on, the early wall of waiting came from the first research taking up to two hours, that's going down to two minutes, and the combat speed is the third time I hear it, so that's next. The chest after every upgrade is a great point, fewer but bigger chests makes a lot of sense. And youre right that the resources need a reason to care, I'll show what each one is for when you first get it. Really appreciate you playing.

comments.author: ItsDumi
comments.body:
Damn that's a lot of playtests dude, good data

If not, at the end of your demo (I didn't play it so idk how long it is) you should add a review form that's just a link to a Google form so they can drop feedback. Especially for the 15 who stayed. Maybe push the form to them

replies.body: Most of them play without an account, so no, I can't reach them, I only see where they stop. A short feedback prompt for the ones who stay is a really good idea though, especially after the first session when they still remember what confused them. Adding that, thanks!

comments.author: TheCelestialBubble
comments.body:
Are the 60 players just randomers who found your game? That's a little important. I haven't tried your game, but it is worth making sure complexity is the issue before investing real time into adjusting that. Some people just may genuinely not like your game, and some of those may be because they don't like the genre, and others may be because your game is not particularly good (I'm not saying it isn't very good to be clear, but that it's possible).

*pre-sending edit* if I've misinterpreted your gameplay, the following is completely useless

I did click on the link and it looks like that Evony/DoA style of game. Normally those are heavy pay to play games... Im assuming as you have no accounts there's no transactions but if there are that can be off putting. I think locking systems as you suggest is the right thing. Typically, in my experience, everything is ultimately locked by the level of your castle or player. It's quite an easy way to balance I think. For example, you can only build certain troops (say giants) once your upgrade a building to a certain level (say your barracks), but that barracks level is locked by your castle level. You castle level takes real world time to upgrade and tons of resources which are difficult to harvest.

replies.author: Curious_Ad5417
replies.body:
Mostly strangers, yes. Almost all came from posts like this one and a few game portals, plus a handful of testers for the Android version. And you're right that some just won't like the genre, that's fine.

On the pay to win worry, fair question for this kind of game. There no real money shop live right now, and when there is one, my own rule is that the gap between free and paying players stays small. I've played enough games where your wallet is the real castle level.

And yes, thats pretty much how it works already, the keep level gates almost everything else. Good to hear that feels right to someone who knows the genre.

comments.author: FazedEclipse2
comments.body:
Honest answer

No truly deep game that's "successful" ever really starts "deep" you have to introduce mechanics.

replies.author: Curious_Ad5417
replies.body: Agreed, and I think that's where I went wrong early on. I was so excited about all the systems that I wanted to show them off on day one. Now its one thing at a time. Out of curiosity, how slow would you go? One new system a day, or tied to progress no matter how long it takes?

replies.author: FazedEclipse2
replies.body: I'd genuinely look at your gameplay loop how it functions, how it functions before mechanics, that would be a tutorial style step then as the game progresses and you earn more things you add tutorials for these. They can be in canon tutorials you don't have to blur the lines. But ultimately, understanding the loop, understanding how each knew addition affects that loop what it gives you etc those are learning steps that might lose a player if not there in the first place.

replies.author: Curious_Ad5417
replies.body: Thats a really useful way to put it, thanks. Teach the loop first, then every new system gets its own small lesson when it unlocks, and ideally the story is the one teaching it. I already have a story that moves forward with the keep level, so tying each new system to a chapter feels like the natural next step. Appreciate you taking the time.

About the screen before the first hunt, was it more that you didnt know what to tap, or that you didnt understand why you were hunting in the first place?

replies.author: Curious_Ad5417

comments.author: RUSuper
comments.body:
I will tell my opinion as I got into it...

First thing... it doesn't hook you instantly... that is most important thing, you have to hook player right away, the way you do it can be done differently, but this doesn't. You can do it with nice visuals, or with interesting "I'm OP" kind of start, or story wise or something... This... you throw me against a monster, it is auto battle that I have to watch, but it is not particularly pleasing to the eye to watch and gameplay wise I don't have to do much. So with todays people focus span I bet they leave on the first fight.

If you want it to make "auto battler" it needs better graphics right away, pleasing to the eye. Sounds are good, they were like "ok it sounds nice" but that will not keep me from leaving, they are just a requirement to have. 

I don't expect your UI to be particularly good if you are new to this, but it just is screaming AI to me, obviously with experience that will come also, you might want to do custom arts for your UI (borders, background textures etc). But that is not what drive people away (well maybe some of them), I just mention it on the side.

Then for example chest... you get the chest, while chest art is ok, there is nothing behind it, not sound to follow the opening, no background. In today world people need that dopamine hook all the time, give them something, at least a sound of anticipation "hey what is there", hook them up with something nice early on like "hey I got this cool thing" that is instantly recognisable (either by colour scheme of items or something visually looking cool) because leather and aether crystal tell me nothing.

Anyway what I want to say is, right now you are betting that people will play long enough game to like the gameplay side of thing, but you can't bet on that, if you don't hook player right away in today's world - they are gone. It's a reality of things. I wish you luck 🤗

replies.author: Curious_Ad5417
replies.body: Thank you, this is honestly the most useful comment Ive had, because you actually played and named the exact moments. The chest point hits home, opening it should feel like something, and leather is not a reward anyone gets excited about. Same with the first fight being something you just watch. Can I ask what would have hooked you in that first minute? More control in the fight, or something that makes you feel powerful right away?

replies.author: RUSuper
replies.body:
Either more control in the fight or just pleasing graphics.

Take Raid Shadows Legends for example. It is now old game and it is extremely predatory but bunch of people played it. For the time it had amazing mobile graphics and fight that tells you like “hey here are your champion few abilities press XYZ to use them” and it was interesting enough combined with good graphics.

replies.author: Curious_Ad5417
replies.body: Thats a clear way to put it, thanks. The game is built for checking in a few times a day, so later fights run on their own while youre away. But the first fights could be the ones where youre in control and trigger a couple of abilities yourself, so you actually feel what your hunter can do before it goes automatic. Going to try that.

replies.author: RUSuper
replies.body: Every auto battler is built this way, they make you play manually before you can use “auto” and do it passively, even tycoon games do it (make you play first hour or two before going afk grind mode) so that is a proven concept 🤷‍♂️

replies.author: Curious_Ad5417
replies.body: Thanks, thats really helpful to hear from someone who knows the genre this well. Maybe Im a bit different as a player, I always enjoyed getting to play my way quickly. In my game the real choices are in the gear you forge, not in the fight itself, so I'll keep the manual part short, a few fights where you feel the difference your gear makes, then it runs on its own. Really appreciate you sticking around in the thread.

replies.author: RUSuper
replies.body: No problem, a proper feedback can go a long way. But also keep in mind… even the best game ever nobody will play if they didn’t hear about it. In today’s world posting game once on Reddit and hoping for players to start playing it is same as hoping to win a lottery, you probably need to be consistent with your updates. I do it weekly.

replies.author: Curious_Ad5417
replies.body: Completely agree, and thats exactly what I learned the hard way. My first post here brought players for three days and then it went quiet. So weekly it is, tonight comments already gave me enough to work on until the next one. Thanks again, this thread has been more useful than anything Ive read about game dev in months.

comments.author: Ganiam

I played a bit

Battle animation is so slow

Mostly there’s not much gameplay or strategy and if I can’t do anything after 10min I’m not going to wait an hour to come back. I’m going to forget about the game completely in that time

replies.author: Curious_Ad5417
replies.body: Thank you for playing and being blunt, thats exactly what I need. An hour of waiting within the first ten minutes is a real problem, not a feature. Do you remember which objective it was? A building, a research, or one of the tasks? I want to make sure nobody hits a wall that early. And noted on the battle speed, that's the second time I hear it tonight.

replies.author: Ganiam
replies.body:
The battle speed is so weird because it takes forever to get to the monster, the hit is super slow, and then there’s like 5 seconds of nothing before another slow swing. 

The 1h thing was the story quests and subquest, 1h each

This type of game needs to make the player feel really good and invested for at least 60-90min before the timers get in the way. The countdown timers have to very slowly increase in time and they have to be staggered so even when it’s 20-30min you still do something every 5-10min.

Otherwise we immediately lose interest. After 90min we are usually invested

replies.author: Curious_Ad5417
replies.body: This is gold, thank you for coming back with a screenshot. You’re right, that’s the story steps, and an hour in chapter one is way too early. comments.author: ThreeDMK
comments.body:
Are you running simulations against your gameplay to measure engagement?

For the one game of mine that includes content being played over time, I have bots simulating the gameplay and identifying when things stay balanced vs trailing off.  I also have the bots configured with different play styles.  These will run the game in a time compressed state.  Example:  idle clicker running at 100x or 1000x.

This shows me where different parts of my game hold up vs drop off.  Will resources collected at one point remain viable later on.  Will players have enough money.  Will there be enough quest content to keep people engaged.  Is there enough to do so that things do not feel repetitive.

Things like this will help you balance the content.  The thing it doesn’t fix is if the game is actually fun.  You can measure wait times, process times, etc, to see where a player will be spending most of their activity, but if those actions do not give that hit of dopamine, you need to revisit it and make changes.

I track rewards as well, how often are the players being rewarded for activity.  When does combat feel more engaging?  What happens when I level up.

Sounds like you have all the data you need, just need to collect it and see what it means.

replies.author: Curious_Ad5417
replies.body: Yes, I run a simulated playthrough that plays the economy and progression in compressed time, so I can see when resources pile up or run dry and how far a player gets by day 100 or 400. Your last point is the one that stings though, it tells me if the numbers work, not if it's fun. Tonight's comments are the fun test, and the answer so far is the first ten minutes need more of it. Tracking how often players get rewarded is a great idea, adding that to my list.

replies.author: ThreeDMK
replies.body:
Nice!  I wish you lucks. Sticky is hard to measure and quantify.  Rewards and capabilities can help.  

World of Warcraft.  Knowing I am getting the next level of Fireball is badass, means things will die faster.

Same concept in your game.  What is a player doing.  You bring up a good point though, most of my testing assumes a player is sticking around at least 30-60 minutes.  That initial hook needs to be good.  

Pro tip though, do not let AI make that decision for you, ask for options and explore ideas.  

You got this :)

replies.author: Curious_Ad5417
replies.body: Thanks, really appreciate it! That feeling of "next upgrade means things die faster" is exactly what I want the forge to deliver, I just have to show it earlier. And don't worry about the AI part, it gives me options and I veto half of them. Sometimes it even tells me Im wrong, which is more than most people do.

comments.author: Bavariasnaps
comments.body:
An in-game shop selling gems for €99 doesn't exactly make me want to play. It immediately feels like a typical pay-to-win game, and unfortunately, I don't enjoy those kinds of games.

Maybe it's true that you haven't played many App Store games in recent years, but most people have experienced pay-to-win games by now. They've learned that once you have to pay for in-game currency, the fun starts to disappear. It also becomes obvious that publishers see you as nothing more than a cash cow to be milked.

Even all those free bonuses and rewards you get for doing practically nothing contribute to that impression. It all feels like a typical mobile game designed to shower you with rewards at first, hook you with constant dopamine hits, and eventually squeeze as much money out of you as possible. Instead of making the game feel rewarding, it makes the whole experience feel manipulative and cheap.

On top of that, within the first few minutes, you realize that it's a real-time action game rather than a turn-based one. You don't have different attack skills to choose from, and the game also includes some idle mechanics.

And the combat system might honestly be one of the most boring I've ever seen. You just click? That's it? Where's the strategy, the variety, or any sense of meaningful player interaction? If combat is supposed to be a core part of the game, simply clicking over and over again isn't exactly exciting or engaging.

You're going to lose potential players because not everyone enjoys these gameplay elements. And when you combine them with aggressive monetization, you're giving people even more reasons to quit before they've really started playing.

replies.author: Curious_Ad5417
replies.body: Thats fair, and I think you just showed me something I couldn't see myself. The shop is only a preview right now, nobody can actually buy anything yet, but you're right that a 99 euro pack is the worst possible first impression for a new player. I'm hiding it until it actually matters. On combat, I hear you, just click is the third comment tonight in the same direction. Thanks for taking the time to write all of it.

comments.author: Harlan_42
comments.body:
If you got to explain it that much, I probably wouldn't be interested.  Also, your examples should be achievement oriented instead of challenge; I think people are looking for the journey, the accomplishment.  You can slay the mighty dragon, or you can battle a mighty dragon.  People now come in with expectations, so you better deliver and quick on at least one goal.  Go with the role playing, and what shall we call our great warrior.  Which shield will you pledge your loyalty kind of thing...get them in the role.  The town is the money shot, you don't want to separate to another page for training or overview, maybe those should be popups that overlay exposing the town around the edges so player doesn't do a full review when panels disappear.  
Went to the town, the info popups maybe should say "Level #" and look different if new level is available.  It should take time to do these level changes, I flew through a bunch thinking so what.  Announcements of completions caused they waited till next session, because they have a reason to come back.  Sometime people need little prompts, so maybe a popup reminder of something to do if no activity for a period of time.  
Maybe you should put them directly into the hunt to let them get a kill and then return to the town. Coach the attack so they know how to battle.  And put the warrior behind the trees, the whatever it was seemed kind of cheesy.    
Not really my kind of game, but if you got them in to look, then make it an experience they want to come back to play.

replies.author: Curious_Ad5417
replies.body: Thank you for actually going through it and writing all this down, thats a lot of useful detail. The town being the money shot is a great way to put it, and youre right that jumping to separate pages pulls you out of it. Same with level ups feeling like nothing, they should feel earned. Noting all of it, especially the role playing angle at the start. Appreciate it even though it's not your kind of game.

comments.author: Reckonerxy

replies.author: Curious_Ad5417

comments.author: bunnyUFO
comments.body:
I'm going to be brutally honest. I opened the game and immediately thought "this is one of those mobile build a base whatever games, probably not for me". Kept going just to give you feedback.

I get to the first few screens thinking "Yup not interested, seems generic" The bad glass/metal clunk sound effect  hits, but keep going.

Then the cutscene with terriby animated, weird graphics hits and I've had enough.

The issue isn't that the game is complex, it's doing a lot to make the player disinterested. I was willing enough to actually play test and get to gameplay, but the sounda and graphics were genuinely off-putting to me.

I'm probably not your target audience, but if the lack of effort for music and grohics wasn't so in my face I might have stuck around a bit more.

replies.author: Curious_Ad5417

You're the third person tonight calling out the sound, so thats getting replaced right away, and the first hunt cutscene clearly isnt doing the job I hoped it would. Fair point that its not the complexity that loses people first, its the first impression. Thats a really useful distinction.

comments.author: SeasawPhilosopher
comments.body: Sorry but I’m not going to take the time to play it, I looked and it’s not really the type of game I’m into. I will say I think you may be mistaken about what makes a game deep. Depth is created by systems complexity, optionality, simulation, strategy, emergence, etc. Your post text implies there is a lot of content not a lot of depth.

replies.author: Curious_Ad5417
replies.body: No need to apologize, and thats a fair correction. Reading my post again, I listed a lot of stuff, and a long list of stuff is content, not depth. The real question is whether the systems push on each other and leave you choices that matter, and that's harder to show in a post than to count things. Good distinction, I'll keep it in mind for the next one.

comments.author: wewerecreaturres
comments.body: You have to build up to the complexity. Teach a new thing, then add it to the mix.

replies.author: Curious_Ad5417
replies.body: Agreed, and thats the rule Im trying to follow now. Most systems already stay locked until your keep gets there, but I opened them too fast and showed too much at once. One example from this week, your first chest now gives you a sword and puts it on right away, so you learn what gear does before anyone shows you the forge. Next I'm cleaning up the hunt screen so a new player only sees the first beast instead of everything at once.

comments.author: Cute_Ad8981
comments.body:
i opened the game and was not sure what to expect. im not sure if this will help you:  

i randomly started the first fight and it was boring for me. i think im generally not a fan of this genre (medieval city building +  browser style + no deep battles). i did not feel a big depth in the battles. they felt slow and not impressive.  

the animations, sounds and overall graphics were nice. 

the menu was confusing. i was receiving gifts, but not understanding for what? 

i saw i could build something, so i looked on the map and could not find deticated places. this is were i personally decided to close the game.

the ressources displayed at the top were displayed in two lines. second line showed only one ressource. this made a ai impression, because ai loves to do such things. (bad ui optimization for different screens)

replies.author: Curious_Ad5417
replies.body:
This helps a lot, thank you. Not being a fan of the genre and still writing all this down is generous.

The resource bar is a fair hit. One lonely resource on its own line looks sloppy, and on some screen widths thats exactly what happens. I'll fix that.

The building part is the one that worries me most. You saw you could build, went to the map and found nowhere to put it. If that's where you closed the game, others probably did the same, so I'll make the first building spot impossible to miss.

Same with the gifts. Right now they just show up without a reason, I'll add a line saying what each one is for.

And noted on the battles, youre the fourth person saying they feel slow. That one's coming.

comments.author: Some-Ice-4455
comments.body: Is it on steam?

replies.author: Curious_Ad5417
replies.body: Not on Steam, its built as a mobile game. You can play it right in the browser at [grauwacht.web.app](http://grauwacht.web.app), on PC too, no download needed. The Android app is in testing on Google Play and should go public in the next days.

comments.author: kronendgames
comments.body: I don´t know, seems like too much of everything else in the same style of game that are thousands in any play store. What would keep me playing that is so different than others?

replies.author: Curious_Ad5417
replies.body: Fair question, and honestly the genre is crowded. What Im trying to do differently, the gap between free and paying players stays small, so your time and your choices matter more than your wallet. Theres a real story told in chapters, with clues to search and decisions that stick. And the heart of it is the hunt, 60 beasts that each want the right blade and oil, so the forge is where you actually think. Whether that's enough to stand out, I'm still finding out. Thats partly why I'm here asking.

replies.author: kronendgames
replies.body: To be honest I don´t think it is enough. I think there should many original things to draw public attention, in the way of collecting resources, building, mechanics, etc. Even though you have some different things, the essential feels to me like any other from the genre.

replies.author: Curious_Ad5417
replies.body: You might be right. The building and collecting part is familiar on purpose, and the things that set it apart only show up later, which doesnt help in the first minutes. Out of curiosity, is there one mechanic you've never seen in this genre that would make you look twice? Im collecting ideas.

replies.author: kronendgames
replies.body: I don´t know I think the genre as u said is overcrowded. Is hard to think in a sole mechanic that would make your game differential. It should be a mayor group of things that make it really stand out, and that is a lot of creativity and work.

replies.author: Curious_Ad5417
replies.body: Agreed, no single trick fixes it. Its a lot of small things stacking up, and the creativity and work part is the bit I actually enjoy. Thanks for sticking with the thread, it gave me a lot to think about.

comments.author: Secure-Map-7538
comments.body:
Tried it and closed it after 20 seconds. 
Looks ugly and lifeless as hell. UI and assets scream single prompt full AI development.

Dont try to cater to people that dont like your game idea but focus on the people that love it and improve it for them. You will never please everyone.

Good games 
start out easy and 
add complexity over time.

replies.author: Curious_Ad5417
replies.body: Thanks for giving it a go. The part about building for the people who like it hits home, I’ve been trying to answer every comment and that pulls the game in all directions. What did you get to see in those 20 seconds, the intro page or already the town?
